book.title: The Millionaire Next Door
book.author: Thomas J. Stanley and William D. Danko

confidence_note: Figures come from Wikipedia and reader notes (8.4 hours/month for middle-income PAWs, about 83 percent more than UAWs); the original text was not accessible. The old text's 8 hours versus 2 hours and the tax/insurance savings claims are not in the book and were rejected. The Willis anecdote comes from a secondary summary. Survivorship-bias criticism by Taleb noted.
facts: The authors call people with high net worth for their income and age PAWs (Prodigious Accumulators of Wealth) and those with low net worth for their income UAWs (Under Accumulators).
PAWs spend nearly twice as many hours a month planning their investments as UAWs (about 83 percent more); among middle-income PAWs the figure is about 8.4 hours a month.
UAWs often say they will start investing once they earn roughly ten percent more income, and usually do not.
Mr. Willis was a Walmart executive for ten years and bought no shares of the company during its growth, although he had the knowledge to do so.
scene_details: 8.4 hours a month on investment planning
Mr. Willis, ten years at Walmart, no shares
the promise to invest after a ten percent raise
tension: A man with inside knowledge of a fast-growing company bought none of it, while the people who built wealth spent nearly twice the hours on their investments.
opening_idea: Open with Mr. Willis: ten years at Walmart during its growth, no shares bought.

lessons.idea: Wealth follows attention to money, not only income; time given to planning is part of the mechanism.
lessons.anchor: PAWs spent nearly twice as many monthly hours on investments as UAWs

reflect_final: If you set aside a fixed hour this month to look at your own money, what is the one decision you would finally make in it?

use_cases.situation: A partner says there is no time for the budget
use_cases.move: Mention that the book's accumulators spent about eight hours a month on investments, and propose one fixed hour on a set evening.

use_cases.situation: You keep saying you will invest after the next raise
use_cases.move: Book one hour in your calendar this week and pick one amount to move now.

use_cases.situation: A colleague mentions company stock options they never looked at
use_cases.move: Ask how long it would take to read the terms, and offer to compare notes after you both do.

pocket_idea: Mr. Willis knew Walmart from inside and bought nothing; knowing is not the same as acting on it.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: A Walmart executive for ten years bought no Walmart shares while the company grew.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Stanley and Danko found that people who built wealth spent nearly twice as many hours on their investments each month, about eight for the middle-income group, while others promised to start after a ten percent raise. One Walmart executive never bought a share in ten years.
